title: Aggression of the newly invasive white-footed ant, Technomyrmex difficilis (Hymenoptera: Formicidae), against native and nonnative ant species in Texas
content:
Abstract
Technomyrmex difficilis Forel (Hymenoptera: Formicidae), the white-footed ant, is an arboreal tramp ant native to Madagascar, recently introduced to Texas at the Texas State Aquarium in Corpus Christi. To evaluate the ecological consequences of potential establishment, interspecific aggression between T. difficilis and 8 heterospecific ant species—5 nonnative and 3 native to Texas—was assessed across 3 group sizes of live workers (1 vs. 1, 5 vs. 5, 10 vs. 10) using laboratory bioassays. A nestmate control and a geographically distinct conspecific pairing (T. difficilis Texas vs. Florida) were included. Aggression was scored on a 5-point scale, and 2 metrics were analyzed: peak aggression per trial and rep-level interval means across fifteen 20 s observation intervals. All heterospecific matchups elicited significantly elevated aggression relative to the nestmate control, with nonnative species provoking stronger responses. Rep-level interval means indicated that aggressive behaviors were more reliably provoked at larger group sizes, though native species elicited less consistent aggression. Technomyrmex difficilis responses were predominantly passive and defensive. The conspecific Texas vs. Florida pairing did not differ from the control, suggesting supercolony-like potential between geographically separated populations. These results indicate that T. difficilis poses a competitive threat to Texas ant communities, though its passive behavior suggests it would struggle in direct combat against more aggressive species such as Solenopsis invicta Buren. Once established, T. difficilis would likely achieve greater worker densities than competitors through polygyne reproductive biology and polydomous colony structure, displacing competitors through resource monopolization rather than direct aggression.
